title: Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens (MP, MT)
short: MP: from p → q and p, infer q. MT: from p → q and ¬q, infer ¬p. The letters can stand for any formulas.
trouble: Learners apply MP with the consequent instead of the antecedent (affirming the consequent), or apply MT to ¬p instead of ¬q.

blocks.html: The first two rules of inference are the two valid conditional forms from Valid and Invalid Argument Forms: modus ponens and modus tollens. In a proof they are written MP and MT.

head: Rule
From
Infer
blocks.cap: The letters stand for any formulas, simple or compound.

blocks.html: MP: from a conditional and its antecedent, infer its consequent. MT: from a conditional and the negation of its consequent, infer the negation of its antecedent. Each cites two lines.

MP is valid because the only row that makes $p \to q$ true and $p$ true also makes $q$ true. MT is valid because if $q$ is false and $p \to q$ is true, $p$ cannot be true (that would make the conditional T → F). Because these are forms, $p$ and $q$ can be replaced by any formulas: from $(r \land s) \to \neg t$ and $r \land s$, MP gives $\neg t$.

blocks.title: A short proof
blocks.q: Premises: $p \to q$, $q \to r$, $\neg r$. Prove $\neg p$.

blocks.html: Applying MP with the consequent instead of the antecedent (from $p o q$ and $q$, inferring $p$), or applying MT with $ eg p$ (from $p o q$ and $ eg p$, inferring $ eg q$). Those are affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent, the two invalid look-alikes. A check: MP needs the part before the arrow; MT needs the negation of the part after it.

MT needs the exact negation of the consequent. If the consequent is $
eg t$, MT needs $
eg 
eg t$. If you have $t$ instead, you will be able to turn it into $
eg 
eg t$ later with a rule of replacement (DN).

The order of the cited lines does not matter: "MP 1, 3" and "MP 3, 1" say the same thing. What matters is that one cited line is a conditional and the other is exactly its antecedent (for MP) or exactly the negation of its consequent (for MT). "Exactly" means the very same formula, not one that merely says the same thing.
Most proofs you will meet use MP somewhere. When you see a conditional among the premises, ask at once: do I have, or can I get, its antecedent (for MP) or the negation of its consequent (for MT)?
